system_prompt:
You are extracting load-bearing passages from one chapter of a guitar method book.

The user will give you the verbatim text of one chapter. Extract every passage
that does any of the following:

- teaches a technique (how to play, fingering, hand position, picking pattern)
- defines a concept (a chord type, a scale, a position system, a terminology)
- gives a rule (when to do X, what to avoid, what to prefer)
- shows a load-bearing example (an exercise that illustrates a method's
  characteristic move)

Output a JSON object with this shape:

  { "quotes": [
      { "topic": "<short topic label>",
        "verbatim_quote": "<exact substring of the input>",
        "why_load_bearing": "<one sentence on why this passage matters>",
        "page": <int, optional>
      },
      ...
  ] }

CRITICAL RULES:
1. `verbatim_quote` MUST be an EXACT substring of the input text. Do not
   paraphrase. Do not add words. Do not fix typos. Copy character-for-character.
2. If you can't find a substantial passage in the input that fits a topic,
   skip the topic — don't fabricate.
3. Skip prose that is purely biographical, motivational, or transitional.
   Keep prose that teaches.
4. Aim for 3-15 quotes per chapter. A chapter with only one load-bearing
   passage gets one quote; a dense chapter gets many.
5. `topic` is a short label (2-6 words). Use the book's own terminology
   when possible.
6. `why_load_bearing` is one sentence in YOUR voice explaining the
   significance — not a paraphrase of the quote.

How to use this book
Although a big part of this method is exclusively dedicated to the guitar, (because it refers to
chord construction and basic visualization of the guitar fretboard),it was created as a tool for all
instruments of all levels (beginner, intermediate and advanced). However, even if you are an
advanced player, make sure you know start at the beginning of the book, otherwise you will
easily get lost by the end of the book.


This method should be used as a dictionary of ideas and techniques. It's important to understand
that the way we approach the musical concepts, ideas and techniques presented here are unique
and cannot be found elsewhere.


Do not worry about learning everything from every chapter. You can go ahead as soon as you
understand the concepts. But always remember that you can come back to any chapter of any
book in order to learn more about a determined subject you want to study again.


Be careful when trying to learn too much at one time. Music is not about quantity but quality.


George and I have been working for many years on this giant collection of books to give you the

The Secret of the Giant Lines
                                                                                               4668




This is one of the most important chapters of this method. From now on, we will be
building single line ideas connecting all the “tools” we have learned previously, such as
scales, arpeggios, scale arpeggios and other ideas. This concept makes the improvisation
much more interesting and unpredictable. We will call this type of single line melodies:
The Giant Lines. To clarify this idea we can deBine them by two things:

a) It must contain at least two bars using 16th notes.
b) It has to combine at least two different scales
Although we study "The Giant Lines" containing two, three, and sometimes four or more,
bars when we apply them we can stop whenever we need to or want to. The Giant Lines
are just a tool to help us memorize single lines and also study technique and articulation.



Static Giant Lines
Static Giant Lines are the combination of many types of scales and arpeggios played over a
single chord simultaneously. However, we must be cautious when playing over dominant
7th chords because they can be found in 3 different situations. Let’s use D7 as an example:

• 1st Situation: Non Leading Dominant Chords in Tonal Songs
                              68


Non leading dominant 7th chords are those that do not lead to any other chord in a tonal
song. They are usually found over the degrees: II, IV, bVI. In these cases we should not use
any “color” (scale) from its dominant (A7), but a combination of dominant scales. The
                     46




example below can clarify what we are talking about:


 4
 4       Cmaj7                      D7                          Dmi7              G7
          I                         II                          IIm               V7
In this progression of chords we have D7 as the IInd degree of “C”. Therefore we can use a
combination of dominant scales such as: “D” Mixolydian, “D” Lydian Dominant and the “D”
blues scale.
We can also add the “D” dominant diminished or “D” Whole Tone scale as two more “colors”
to improvise with.
